summary: Describes an IP/MPLS network whose infrastructure is split into strata, with one stratum for "Hard Pipes" and another for normal IP/MPLS traffic. A Hard Pipe is an MPLS LSP or pseudowire with guaranteed bandwidth. The document is architectural and informational.

eli5.summary: Think of a road with a private lane that always has room for one special truck, while everyone else shares the normal lanes.

subtitle: Reserving guaranteed bandwidth in IP/MPLS networks

tldr.problem: Operators want to offer leased-line services over IP/MPLS networks with the same guaranteed bandwidth characteristics as traditional TDM networks, but normal IP/MPLS uses statistical multiplexing where bandwidth is not guaranteed.
tldr.mechanism: Stratify the network into two logical strata: one for Hard Pipes (MPLS LSPs and pseudowires with reserved bandwidth) that forbids overbooking, and one for normal IP/MPLS traffic that uses the remaining capacity.
tldr.outcome: Operators can retire expensive TDM networks while offering equivalent services, using existing MPLS standards without new protocols, with bandwidth guaranteed end-to-end.

today: RFC 7625 is an Informational RFC that describes an operational architecture deployed by vendors and network operators to support leased-line services. It has not been obsoleted and remains relevant for operators seeking to migrate from TDM to packet networks.

sections.title: The Hard Pipe Concept
sections.content:
This document describes a practical architecture for offering leased-line services—Virtual Leased Line (VLL) and equivalent services—over IP/MPLS networks while maintaining the bandwidth guarantees that customers expect. A Hard Pipe is an MPLS Label Switched Path (LSP) or pseudowire (PW) with reserved bandwidth that is neither exceeded nor infringed upon by other traffic.

The key insight is that a single physical network can be divided into two logical strata. The Hard Pipe stratum reserves a fixed amount of bandwidth per link and operates without statistical multiplexing—if bandwidth is allocated to a leased line, that bandwidth is guaranteed end-to-end. The Normal IP/MPLS stratum gets the remaining bandwidth and operates as a conventional IP/MPLS network. Routers handle traffic from the two strata differently, based on label ranges set aside in hardware for Hard Pipes.
sections.eli5: Hard Pipes are like reserved lanes on a highway: some lanes are kept free for emergency vehicles or special delivery trucks, and other lanes are used by everyone else.

sections.title: Network Stratification
sections.content:
The physical network is shared, but the resource allocation is distinct. An operator first estimates the traffic matrix—how much traffic will flow between each pair of routers—and then decides how much bandwidth to allocate to the Hard Pipe stratum on each link. For example, a 10 Gbps link might be split into 4 Gbps for Hard Pipes and 6 Gbps for normal IP/MPLS traffic.

Each stratum becomes a separate logical network. Hard Pipes are configured using a defined set of labels that routers reserve exclusively for the Hard Pipe application. The Normal IP/MPLS stratum uses different labels and can operate independently. Because the strata are logically separated with distinct resources, congestion or overbooking in the Normal IP/MPLS stratum cannot affect the Hard Pipe stratum.
sections.eli5: It is like splitting a road into a private lane for guaranteed service and a public lane for everyone else. They share the same pavement but have different rules.

sections.title: Setting Up Leased Lines
sections.content:
When an operator receives a request for a leased line, the Network Management System (NMS) or controller checks whether a path exists in the Hard Pipe stratum that can accommodate the requested bandwidth. If such a path exists and a tunnel (created with T-labels) is available, the operator assigns a Leased Line label (L-label) at the ingress and egress routers to establish the service. The available bandwidth for that path is decremented in the global resource table.

If no tunnel is available, a new one is created. If the path cannot be expanded to meet the request, the leased line setup is declined. The process is simple: two steps of label configuration, with all state information kept in the NMS/Controller rather than on the routers. This minimizes the processing burden on routers and allows efficient management of the network's growing resource usage.
sections.eli5: Setting up a leased line is like booking a reserved section of highway from point A to point B: the operator checks if that section is free, reserves it, and tells the routers how to use it.

sections.title: Efficient State Tracking
sections.content:
The architecture minimizes the amount of state stored on routers (the Label Switching Routers, or LSRs). Each router only needs to know: the label-swapping operations (incoming label to outgoing label and port), whether a label belongs to the Hard Pipe set, and the available bandwidth per stratum on each of its links. Everything else—topology, bandwidth resources, tunnel mappings, and leased line mappings—resides in the centralized NMS/Controller.

This centralized approach simplifies operation and scaling. The NMS/Controller tracks total and available bandwidth per link, the mappings between tunnel labels and leased-line labels, and the reserved bandwidth for each leased line. When a leased line is added or removed, only the NMS/Controller updates its global resource table; routers receive only the label configuration commands they need to apply.
sections.eli5: Instead of giving every router a complete rulebook, the central control system tells each router only the few rules it needs to handle traffic correctly.

sections.title: Protection and High Availability
sections.content:
The document specifies that leased lines use the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) linear protection mechanisms, defined in RFCs 6378, 7271, and 7324. These mechanisms enable operations like Continuity Check (CC) and Connection Verification (CV) to run over the tunnels between the endpoints of each leased line. The entire tunnel is protected end-to-end, ensuring that link failures are detected and traffic is rerouted to protection paths.

MPLS-TP Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) procedures apply to Hard Pipe tunnels, allowing operators to monitor the health of leased lines and respond to faults. This is essential for meeting the Service Level Agreements (SLAs) that customers expect from leased-line services.
sections.eli5: If a reserved lane gets damaged, the system automatically detects the problem and moves traffic to a backup lane, keeping the service running.
